topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Areas and Heron's formula
topic.scope: area of triangle by Heron's formula, area of quadrilaterals

nodes.name: Area of triangles
external_prereqs: area of a triangle as half base times height

nodes.name: Area = half base times corresponding height
Height is perpendicular to the base
Right triangle: legs serve as base and height
Subtract each side from s separately
Take the square root at the end
Heron's formula works for every triangle
Sides must be in the same unit
Sides given as a ratio need a multiplier
A diagonal splits a quadrilateral into two triangles
Total area is the sum of the triangle areas
Rhombus area is half product of diagonals
external_prereqs: diagonals of a rhombus bisect at right angles

nodes.name: Parallelogram area is base times height, not slant side

misconceptions.statement: The area of a triangle is base times height, with no half.
misconceptions.why: Students blend the rectangle rule with the triangle rule.
misconceptions.fix: A triangle is half of a parallelogram or rectangle on the same base and height, so its area is ½ × base × height.

probe.question: A triangle has base 10 cm and height 6 cm. What is its area?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one shape works for all shapes
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student errors in area measurement formulas

misconceptions.statement: The height of a triangle is always one of its sides.
misconceptions.why: Students mostly see right-angled or upright triangles drawn on a horizontal base.
misconceptions.fix: The height is the perpendicular distance from a vertex to the opposite side, and it usually lies inside the triangle, not along a side.

probe.question: A triangle has sides 5, 5 and 6 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm on the base 6 cm. What height do you use?
probe.wrong_answer: 5 cm, because it is a side

misconceptions.root_belief: a typical picture is the only possible case
misconceptions.source_hint: research on prototype images and height of triangles and parallelograms

misconceptions.statement: Height can be measured along any slanting side.
misconceptions.why: Students treat any length from the vertex to the base line as the height.
misconceptions.fix: Height must make a right angle with the base. A slanting side is longer than the height and gives a wrong area.

probe.question: A parallelogram has base 8 cm, slant side 5 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm. What is its area?

misconceptions.root_belief: any length that looks similar is the same measure
misconceptions.source_hint: research on area formulas for parallelograms

misconceptions.statement: The area of a triangle can be written in cm or m.
misconceptions.why: Students mix length units with area units.
misconceptions.fix: Area counts squares, so it is written in square units such as cm² or m².

probe.question: Give the unit of the area of a triangle with sides in cm.

misconceptions.root_belief: all measures use the same kind of unit
misconceptions.source_hint: research on area versus perimeter and units

misconceptions.statement: The area of an equilateral triangle of side a is a²/2.
misconceptions.why: Students copy the square or right-triangle shortcut.
misconceptions.fix: The height of an equilateral triangle is (√3/2)a, so the area is (√3/4)a².

probe.question: Find the area of an equilateral triangle of side 4 cm.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: In an isosceles triangle, the area is half of the equal side times the base.
misconceptions.why: Students use the two sides they can see as base and height.
misconceptions.fix: Find the height using Pythagoras on half the base, then use ½ × base × height, or use Heron's formula.

probe.question: Find the area of an isosceles triangle with equal sides 5 cm and base 6 cm.

misconceptions.root_belief: given numbers should be multiplied directly

misconceptions.statement: Heron's formula is required for a right-angled triangle.
misconceptions.why: Students think the new formula replaces all earlier ones.
misconceptions.fix: In a right triangle the two legs are base and height, so ½ × leg × leg is simpler, though Heron's formula also gives the same answer.

probe.question: Which is the quickest way to find the area of a triangle with sides 6, 8 and 10 cm?

misconceptions.root_belief: the newest method replaces all earlier methods

misconceptions.statement: In Heron's formula, s means the perimeter.
misconceptions.why: Students mix the letter s with the whole perimeter.
misconceptions.fix: s is the semi-perimeter, which is half the sum of the three sides.

probe.question: Sides are 5, 12 and 13 cm. What is s?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar terms mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student errors with formula symbols and Heron's formula

misconceptions.statement: In s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c), you subtract the sum of the sides from s.
misconceptions.why: Students read the brackets as one subtraction.
misconceptions.fix: Subtract each side from s separately to get s−a, s−b and s−c, then multiply them with s.

probe.question: For sides 5, 12, 13 (s = 15), find the value inside the root.

misconceptions.root_belief: symbols in brackets combine into one operation

misconceptions.statement: Heron's formula is s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c), with the square root applied only to s.
misconceptions.why: Students forget what the root symbol covers.
misconceptions.fix: The square root covers the whole product s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c).

probe.question: Sides 5, 12, 13 (s = 15). Find the area.

misconceptions.root_belief: a symbol applies only to what is next to it

misconceptions.statement: Heron's formula is s(a+b+c) type, the sides are just added and multiplied.
misconceptions.why: Students recall the formula as a pile of symbols.
misconceptions.fix: Heron's formula uses s and the three differences s−a, s−b, s−c, not the sum of sides again.

probe.question: Area of triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 by Heron's formula?

misconceptions.root_belief: memorised formulas need no understanding

misconceptions.statement: The final area is the product under the root, with no root taken.
misconceptions.why: Students stop after computing the product.
misconceptions.fix: The root is the last step. The area is the square root of the product, in square units.

probe.question: For 5, 12, 13 the product is 900. What is the area?

misconceptions.root_belief: the last step of a procedure is optional

misconceptions.statement: The square root of a sum or product splits into separate roots by adding.
misconceptions.why: Students think square root distributes over addition.
misconceptions.fix: √(a+b) is not √a + √b. Multiply the numbers first, then take one root, or factorise into perfect squares.
misconceptions.root_belief: an operation distributes over everything inside brackets
misconceptions.source_hint: research on algebra errors with roots and distribution

misconceptions.statement: Heron's formula works only for scalene triangles.
misconceptions.why: Students see examples with three different sides only.
misconceptions.fix: It works for every triangle: scalene, isosceles, equilateral and right-angled.

probe.question: Can Heron's formula be used for a triangle with sides 5, 5, 6?

misconceptions.root_belief: a method works only for the examples seen

misconceptions.statement: Any three lengths can be the sides of a triangle, so Heron's formula always gives an area.
misconceptions.why: Students never check the triangle inequality.
misconceptions.fix: Each side must be shorter than the sum of the other two. Otherwise a factor s−a becomes zero or negative and no triangle exists.

probe.question: Can sides 2, 3, 8 cm form a triangle with an area given by Heron's formula?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, s = 6.5 and compute the area

misconceptions.root_belief: a formula can be applied without checking conditions
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student reasoning about triangle existence

misconceptions.statement: Sides in m and cm can be put into Heron's formula as they are.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the numbers and ignore units.
misconceptions.fix: Convert all sides to the same unit before finding s, or the answer will be wrong.

probe.question: Sides are 3 m, 400 cm and 5 m. What is s?

misconceptions.root_belief: numbers matter and units do not
misconceptions.source_hint: research on unit conversion errors in measurement

misconceptions.statement: If sides are in the ratio 3:4:5, the sides are 3, 4 and 5 cm.
misconceptions.why: Students treat ratio numbers as actual lengths.
misconceptions.fix: The sides are 3x, 4x and 5x. Use the perimeter to find x first.

probe.question: Sides are in ratio 3:4:5 and perimeter is 60 cm. Find the sides.

misconceptions.root_belief: ratio numbers are the actual quantities
misconceptions.source_hint: research on ratio and proportional reasoning errors

misconceptions.statement: A quadrilateral can be split into triangles only along a diagonal that is inside and equal in length to the other diagonal.
misconceptions.why: Students think of rectangles, where diagonals are equal.
misconceptions.fix: Any diagonal that lies inside the quadrilateral splits it into two triangles. The diagonals do not need to be equal.

probe.question: Can a kite with unequal diagonals be split into two triangles by one diagonal?

misconceptions.root_belief: properties of the usual example hold for all

misconceptions.statement: The area of a quadrilateral is the product of its two triangles' areas.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse combining areas with multiplying.
misconceptions.fix: Areas of parts add up, so the quadrilateral's area is the sum of the two triangle areas.

probe.question: A diagonal splits a quadrilateral into triangles of area 6 cm² and 4 cm². What is its area?

misconceptions.root_belief: combining quantities means multiplying them

misconceptions.statement: A quadrilateral's area can be found from its four sides using Heron's formula directly.
misconceptions.why: Students extend a formula for three sides to four.
misconceptions.fix: Four sides do not fix a quadrilateral's shape. You need a diagonal or an angle to split it into triangles.

probe.question: Sides of a quadrilateral are 3, 4, 5, 6 cm. Find its area using Heron's formula with s = 9.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule for three works for any number

misconceptions.statement: The area of a rhombus is the product of its diagonals.
misconceptions.why: Students drop the half, like in the triangle rule.
misconceptions.fix: A rhombus is made of four congruent right triangles, so its area is ½ × d₁ × d₂.

probe.question: A rhombus has diagonals 8 cm and 6 cm. Find its area.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: research on area formula errors for quadrilaterals

misconceptions.statement: The area of a parallelogram is base times its slant side.
misconceptions.why: Students multiply the two side lengths as for a rectangle.
misconceptions.fix: The area is base × perpendicular height. A parallelogram is not a rectangle, so the slant side is not the height.

probe.question: A parallelogram has sides 10 cm and 6 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm on the 10 cm base. Find its area.

misconceptions.root_belief: every four-sided shape behaves like a rectangle
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' area of parallelograms and rectangle prototypes

misconceptions.statement: Quadrilaterals with the same perimeter have the same area.
misconceptions.why: Students link perimeter and area as one measure.
misconceptions.fix: Different shapes with the same perimeter can have different areas.

probe.question: A square and a long thin rectangle have perimeter 20 cm. Do they have the same area?

misconceptions.root_belief: two related measures always change together
misconceptions.source_hint: research on area and perimeter confusion

misconceptions.statement: Heron's formula needs the height, so it cannot be used before finding it.
misconceptions.why: Students think all triangle area formulas need height.
misconceptions.fix: Heron's formula uses only the three sides, which is why it is useful when height is unknown.

probe.question: Can we find the area of a triangle with sides 7, 8 and 9 cm without its height?

misconceptions.root_belief: one formula is the only way to get a result
